props.title: The Night of the Iguana

sections.content: The Night of the Iguana (1964) represents Tennessee Williams at his most fevered and John Huston at his most psychologically penetrating. Richard Burton delivers a career-defining performance as Rev. Shannon, a defrocked minister leading tours in Mexico while battling his inner demons. The film's sweaty, tropical atmosphere perfectly mirrors the characters' psychological states, much like Huston would later achieve in Wise Blood (1979). The adaptation maintains Williams' signature mix of repressed sexuality, religious crisis, and emotional breakdown that defined his other landmark film adaptations like A Streetcar Named Desire (1951) and Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1958).

sections.content: The film showcases the incredible ensemble work of Ava Gardner, Deborah Kerr, and Sue Lyon - each representing different aspects of feminine sexuality and emotional need that torment Burton's character. Gardner's earthy, experienced Maxine contrasts beautifully with Kerr's repressed Hannah, while Lyon's Charlotte echoes her provocative role in Lolita (1962). Huston's direction emphasizes the tropical Mexican setting as both paradise and purgatory, much as he would later do in The Dead (1987), using location as a character itself. SUBHEAD: Tennessee Williams on Film

The Night of the Iguana marked a turning point in Williams adaptations, moving away from the heavily censored versions of the 1950s toward more faithful interpretations of his work. The film maintains the playwright's complex sexual politics while adding Huston's characteristic psychological realism, setting the stage for later Williams adaptations like The Roman Spring of Mrs. Stone (1961) and Last of the Mobile Hot-Shots (1970). The movie's exploration of spiritual crisis and sexual repression influenced later religious-themed dramas like The Thorn Birds (1983) and Priest (1994).
